cards.text: Taxes are payments you must make to a government. They are not a choice. Three levels of government collect taxes: federal, provincial or territorial, and municipal (your city or town).

image.alt: A wooden box with a slot beside gold discs and a blank paper form

cards.text: There are several kinds of tax. Each one is charged on something different. The table shows six of them.

figure.title: Kinds of tax
rows: Most goods and services you buy
Some goods, such as fuel-inefficient vehicles

cards.text: Property taxes are calculated by municipal (local) governments. They are based on the value of land and buildings. Individuals and businesses pay income tax on their income.

image.alt: A small model house and lawn with a measuring tape and a blank paper tag

cards.text: Excise taxes are imposed on fuel-inefficient vehicles, including station wagons, vans and sport utility vehicles, and on gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation gasoline and aviation fuel. Excise duties are charged on spirits, wine, beer, tobacco, cannabis and vaping products.

image.alt: A fuel can, a bottle and a barrel on a shelf, each with a blank label and a gold disc

cards.text: Some taxes come off your pay. CPP and EI contributions come off an employee's pay. CPP is a retirement pension you could receive at 60 or older after at least one valid contribution. EI pays benefits to people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.

image.alt: A blank pay slip with two gold discs moving toward two plain jars

cards.text: Taxes help pay for education and schools, health care and hospitals, and roads and bridges. The next level looks at the GST, the HST and the PST.

cards.text: The Canada Revenue Agency, or CRA, runs tax laws for the federal government and for most provinces and territories. A tax law is a rule about who pays tax and how much.

image.alt: A stone office building with a blank flag and a desk of blank forms

cards.text: In Alberta, the CRA collects personal income tax together with federal income tax. So an Alberta taxpayer deals with the CRA for both.

image.alt: A blank province map with gold discs and a magnifying glass

cards.text: Canada's system relies on each person filing their own return every year. A return is the form that reports your income and works out your tax.

image.alt: A desk with a blank form, a pen, gold discs and a mug of tea

cards.text: The CRA also pays money out. It runs benefit and incentive programs through the tax system. A benefit is a payment to people who qualify.

image.alt: A mailbox with gold discs spilling onto snow and a blank envelope

cards.text: One benefit is the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, once called the GST/HST credit. It is paid every three months to eligible people.
To continue to receive benefit and credit payments, people must update their information with the CRA each year. They do this by filing their income tax and benefit return.

cards.text: A Social Insurance Number, or SIN, is a nine-digit number you need to work in Canada and to use government programs and benefits. Service Canada issues it.

image.alt: A blank card beside a closed passport cover and a pen on a desk

cards.text: You can apply for a SIN online, by mail, or in person. There is no fee. Anyone 12 years or older can apply for their own SIN.

image.alt: A laptop, a sealed envelope and a small counter with a blank sign

cards.text: To apply, you give the documents the application asks for. One is a birth certificate issued by a vital statistics agency. The list also includes a passport, a provincial or territorial ID card or driver's licence, and other Canadian government ID.

figure.title: Papers for a SIN application
rows: Driver's licence or provincial ID card

cards.text: Employers need your SIN to report your income for tax and social benefits. Financial institutions need your SIN to report income like interest and dividends. Only provide your SIN when the law requires it.

image.alt: A blank clipboard and pay slips with a small bank counter behind

cards.text: Your confirmation of SIN letter and your SIN card are not identity documents. Do not show them to prove who you are.

image.alt: A blank card in a sleeve beside a passport and a licence card

cards.text: Guard your SIN. It is private, and it is illegal for anyone else to use it. Protecting it protects you from fraud and identity theft. Identity theft is when someone uses your details to pretend to be you.

image.alt: A brass padlock on a wooden box with a key on a hook

cards.text: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) has a Taxpayer Bill of Rights. It lists 16 rights that describe how you are entitled to be treated when you deal with the CRA. You do not need to memorise them. Here are the ideas behind a few.

image.alt: An open blank booklet with a ribbon on a desk

cards.text: Some rights are about money. You have the right to "receive entitlements and pay no more and no less than required by law". An entitlement is something the law says you are owed, such as a refund. You also have the right to "relief from penalties and interest because of extraordinary circumstances".

image.alt: A balance scale with gold discs and a blank sheet

cards.text: Some rights are about information. You have the right to "service in both official languages", which means English or French. You have the right to "privacy and confidentiality". And you have the right to "complete, accurate, clear, and timely information".

image.alt: A blank envelope with a padlock beside folders

cards.text: Some rights are about disagreeing. You have the right to "a formal review and a subsequent appeal", and to "be represented by a person of your choice". You can "lodge a service complaint and request a formal review without fear of reprisal". Reprisal means being punished for it.

image.alt: Two empty chairs across a desk with a blank sheet

cards.text: Some rights are about fair treatment. You have the right to "be treated professionally, courteously, and fairly" and to "have the law applied consistently". Unless the law says otherwise, you have the right "not to pay income tax amounts in dispute before an impartial review". Impartial means fair.

cards.text: Rights come with responsibilities. A responsibility is something you are expected to do. levels.title: Ways to file a return
learn: Name the ways to file a return and say what NETFILE is.

cards.text: You can file your own return, or have someone else file it. Your own: tax software, SimpleFile or a paper tax return. Someone else: a professional tax preparer or a volunteer at a free tax clinic.

Tax software that the CRA has certified helps you work out your tax and send your return electronically. NETFILE is the CRA service that carries your return from that software to the CRA over the internet. Software first, then NETFILE.

image.alt: A blank form with a blank slip clipped to it and an envelope

cards.text: A tax preparer, such as an accountant, prepares your return and sends it to the CRA for a fee, using a service called EFILE. A free tax clinic is run by volunteers. They complete returns for people with a modest income and a simple tax situation.

levels.title: The concept in four parts
learn: Name the four parts of a business concept.
Tell a strong concept statement from a weak one.

cards.text: A business concept is a short, clear description of a business idea. It answers four questions. What is the product or service? Who is the customer? What is the benefit? How does the customer get it?

The product or service is what you sell. The customer is who buys it. The person who uses it is not always the person who pays. A club selling art kits to Grade 4 students has two people to think about: the child who uses the kit and the parent who pays.

A feature describes the product. A benefit is what the product does about the customer's problem. Customers buy benefits. Here are three features and benefits for hot chocolate sold at a winter market.

figure.title: Features and benefits
rows: Warms you up while you wait
Does not spill in your bag

cards.text: Distribution is how the product gets to the customer: where and when. A cart by the main doors at 3:15 reaches students who are waiting for the bus. A table in a quiet hallway at 9:00 reaches far fewer of them.

Bus Stop Cocoa sells hot chocolate in lidded cups to students waiting for the bus, so they warm up before the ride home. A cart by the main doors serves them from 3:15 to 3:45. The table pulls the statement apart.

levels.title: Feasibility and the competition
learn: Check whether an idea has a market you can reach.
Read a competitive matrix and name why you win.

cards.text: Feasibility asks whether an idea can work, and it needs evidence. It has three questions. Is there a market? Can you reach it? Why would people pick you over the others?

A market is not the whole school. It is the people in the right place, at the right time, with the right need and money. Oakfield School has 800 students. 70% stay for lunch. Half of those buy anything. A quarter of those would buy a hot drink.

The honest market must be bigger than the break-even point: the number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs. The next unit works it out. If a stand needs 90 sales and its honest market is 70 students, the plan is short of buyers.

Where and when you sell changes who you reach: the lunch line, between classes, after school or at an event. Each has different customers, a different amount of time to buy and different money in their pockets. Sell where your customer already is.

A direct competitor sells the same thing to the same customer. An indirect competitor wins the same dollar another way. Doing nothing is a competitor too, because many students just buy nothing. You win for one honest reason: cheaper, closer, better or different.

A competitive matrix lists competitors side by side with a strength and a weakness for each. Here is the one for Bus Stop Cocoa, which charges $2.00. A team then writes one reason to win for each row, including the row for doing nothing.

cards.text: A survey asks many people a few short questions. Opinions are cheap and polite. Evidence is what a person did, with a number. A survey that gathers opinions mostly tells you people are being nice.

figure.title: Opinion or evidence
rows: I take the bus four days a week
I paid $4 for one at a market

cards.text: Rule 1: ask about the past, not the future. People are poor at predicting what they will do and good at saying what they did. Ask about last week, not next month.

figure.title: Ask about the past
rows: Would you buy a hot drink after school?

cards.text: Rule 2: do not lead. A leading question hints at the answer the asker wants: "Don't you think the vending machine is too dear?" Ask "What do you usually spend at the vending machine?" Offer real choices, so people pick instead of agreeing.

Rule 3: one thing per question. "Would you buy a cheap, warm, healthy snack?" asks three things. A "no" does not say which one. Rule 4: keep it quick. About five questions, mostly multiple choice, and at most one open box.

A short survey needs five answers: do they buy at all, how much do they spend, would they pick you over real alternatives, what price, and what would stop them. For price, offer a choice of prices with a "would not buy" option, because people say they would pay more than they do.

levels.title: Fixed and variable costs
learn: Sort a cost as fixed or variable.
Work out the unit cost and the total cost.

cards.text: Every business has costs. Some stay the same however much you sell. Some grow with every item you sell. Telling them apart is the first step to knowing whether a plan can work.
A fixed cost stays the same however many items are sold. You pay it if you sell 0 or 500. A variable cost grows with each item sold. You only pay it when you make or sell one more.
Mei sells bracelets at a weekend craft fair. The table sorts her costs. The three fixed costs add to $80.00. The variable costs are per bracelet.

The unit cost is the variable cost of one item. Mei adds beads, string and a bag: $0.90 + $0.30 + $0.20 = $1.40. The price must be higher than the unit cost, or a sale puts nothing toward the fixed costs.
Some costs hide in the wrong column. Packaging is variable: each item needs its own. A card fee charged on every sale is variable too. A banner or poster is printed once, so it is fixed.
Total cost = fixed costs + unit cost x items sold. Mei pays $80.00 even if she sells none.

levels.title: Contribution margin and break-even
learn: Work out the contribution margin of one sale.
Find how many items cover the fixed costs.

cards.text: Jo sells iced tea at a school fair for $3.00 a cup. Each cup costs $1.10 in the cup, tea and ice. Jo's fixed costs add to $95.00.

The contribution margin is the price minus the variable cost of one item. $3.00 - $1.10 = $1.90. Each cup sold puts $1.90 toward the fixed costs. It is not profit yet. Profit starts after the fixed costs are paid.
The break-even point is the number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs. Divide the fixed costs by the contribution margin. $95.00 / $1.90 = 50 cups.
Check it. At 50 cups Jo is even. One cup fewer and Jo is short by $1.90. One cup more and Jo makes $1.90. Break-even is the line, not a target to aim at.
A stall cannot sell part of a cup. If the answer has a decimal, round up. Say the fixed costs are $95.00 and the margin is $2.00: 47.5 so 48 cups. At 47 cups the stall is still short.
Check the margin first. If the price only equals the unit cost, the margin is $0.00. No number of sales can cover the fixed costs. If the price is lower, each sale makes the hole deeper.

options.why: 47 items earn $94.00, still less than $95.00.

levels.title: Per day, and what changes
learn: Turn break-even into a number to sell each day.
Say what a new price or cost does to it.

cards.text: Break-even in items is only half the answer. Divide it by the selling days: items ÷ days = items a day. The fair runs 5 days. Jo needs 50 cups, so 50 ÷ 5 = 10 cups a day.

Then ask if that is real. A baker's fixed costs are $360.00 and each loaf leaves $0.90, so 400 loaves. Over 10 days that is 40 a day. If about 50 people pass each day, 40 of 50 is 80%. Four in five must buy.
A lower price cuts the margin, so you need more sales. Jo drops the price by $0.50: the margin is $1.40, and $95.00 / $1.40 = 67.9, so 68 cups. Look at how fast it climbs.
Costs that go up do the same. If a cup costs $1.40 instead of $1.10, the margin is $1.60 and 59.4 rounds up to 60 cups. If the fixed costs rise to $110.00, $110.00 / $1.90 = 57.9, so 58 cups.
Test more than one result. Jo plans to sell 80 cups, so check half of that and half as much again. A plan that works only if everything goes right is a weak plan.

Items you make and do not sell are a cost you have already paid. Jo makes 80 cups and sells 60. The 20 left cost 20 x $1.10 = $22.00. Ways to cut it: a discount on the last day, or smaller batches that are made again when stock runs out.

levels.title: The cost of waiting
learn: Compare two savers who start at different ages.
Say why the early years are worth the most.

cards.text: Alia and Ravi each save $200.00 a month. Alia saves from age 22 to 32, then stops and never adds again. Ravi starts later, at 32, and saves every month until he is 65. Both earn 7% a year in this example. Who has more at 65?
Count what each puts in. Ravi saves for 33 years and Alia for 10. Ravi puts in $55,200 more, over three times as much. But Alia's first deposit has 43 years until 65, and Ravi's has 33.

Interest is added every month, at 7% divided by 12. Each deposit goes in at the end of a month. Every figure is worked out month by month and shown to the nearest dollar. Alia ends $37,600 ahead, the two balances subtracted.

Alia stopped at 32 with $34,617. She added nothing after that, and her balance still climbed to $346,413 by 65, about 10 times as much. Her early deposits had the most years to grow, and the line gets steeper as the interest earns interest.

Now let one saver put in $200.00 every month until 65 and change only the start age. A later start means fewer deposits and less time for each one. The rate matters too: at 5% in this example Ravi finishes ahead, $201,080 to Alia's $161,157.

levels.title: Four kinds of assets
learn: Name the four asset classes and what each one does.
Say what you get and what you risk with each.

cards.text: Many things can hold your money. They behave in a few ways, so they are sorted into four groups called asset classes. An asset is something you own that has value. The class decides what the asset pays you and what can go wrong.

Cash and equivalents are money you can reach quickly, like a savings account. A GIC, a loan to a bank for a set term, sits here too: locked until the term ends, it may pay a bit more for that. The danger is slow: at 3% inflation (an example), a $200.00 basket costs $206.00 next year, while your $200.00 stays $200.00.

Fixed income is lending to a government or a company, which then owes you. A bond is such a loan. It pays a set amount on set dates. Lend $1,000.00 at 5% and a year's payment is $50.00. You lose if the borrower fails to pay, or if prices rise faster than the payment. If a company fails, lenders are paid before owners.

Equities are shares: you own part of a business. Owners are paid last, from what remains. A shop takes in $8,000, pays $5,000 in costs and $500 to its lender, leaving $2,500 for the owners. Sometimes nothing remains. One company is one bet. An index fund holds many companies and spreads it.

Real assets and alternatives hold value in a thing: property and gold, and crypto, which fits nowhere else. The test: does the thing pay you? A shop earns a profit, a bond pays interest, a rented house pays rent. A bar of gold or a crypto coin pays nothing, so its value rests on what the next buyer will pay.

Side by side, each class has its own job. Cash is there for money you need soon. Fixed income pays a set amount. Equities share in what a business earns. Real assets hold value in a thing. The next level combines them into a mix.

cards.text: A mix is how you split money across the four classes. Use 100 points, and each point is 1% of the money. A mix of 20 points in cash, 30 in fixed income, 45 in equities and 5 in real assets and alternatives adds to 100 and puts 45% in equities.

Three made-up people each need money at a different time. Sami needs hers in 10 months. Hana needs hers in 8 years. Lars needs his in 41 years. How long until you need the money is your timeline. It is the first question for a mix.

Why does the timeline matter? Equities can fall, and a fall takes time to repair. In the game's Exchange a teacher can stage a market crash that takes 25% off equity funds and 5% off bond funds. Cash stays the same in dollars. Money needed in 10 months cannot wait out a crash.

This gives a rule. The sooner you need the money, the more weight goes to cash and fixed income. The longer you can wait, the more weight equities can carry. Age is not the rule: Sami is 16 but her timeline is shorter than that of a 63-year-old who retires in 2 years.

Mixes for one timeline can differ and still be reasonable. A person 2 years from retiring may keep some equities or go nearly all cash. The rule gives the direction, not one answer. A second question is personal: how big a drop can you sit through? That is risk tolerance.

The game's Exchange has a fund of every company in town, a bond fund and a balanced fund. The balanced fund holds 60 parts equity fund and 40 parts bond fund, one made-up kind of mix. Look at what each fund holds. Nothing here says what to buy.

cards.text: Risk is how far a result can land from what you hoped for, and how little warning you get. It is not only how much you lost. A choice can be risky even in a year when nothing goes wrong. More chance of loss and bigger swings mean more risk.

Risk tolerance is how big a fall in value a person can live with, without being forced to sell or choosing to sell in a panic. It belongs to the person, not to the investment. Two people can hold the same thing and have different tolerances.

Time is the first thing that shapes it. Lena needs $3,000.00 for school in 8 months. Omar is saving for something 25 years away. A fall hurts Lena more: she has little time to wait before she must spend the money. Omar can leave his alone for years.

Need is the second. Money for rent or a bill due soon must be there on the day. Spare money, with no date it must be spent, can sit through a fall. The same fall matters more for a dollar that has a job to do soon.

How you react is the third. A fall in value is a loss on paper until you sell. Someone who sells in a panic turns it into a real loss. A person who knows they would panic has a lower tolerance, whatever the numbers say. That is honest, not weak.
Here are the three side by side. Each one leans toward more room for risk or less. They describe a person. They do not decide anything for them.

cards.text: A percent change is a percent of the value at that moment, not of the starting value. Take $100.00. A fall of 20% takes off $20.00 and leaves $80.00. A rise of 10% is then 10% of $80.00, which is $8.00. The value is $88.00, not $90.00.
Here is the same case in steps. The 10% rise is measured on a smaller value than the 20% fall was, so it adds fewer dollars than the fall took off.
Equal percents do not cancel. A fall of 25% from $100.00 leaves $75.00. A rise of 25% is measured on $75.00, so it adds $18.75 and gives $93.75. That is still below the start.

To get back, the rise must be bigger than the fall, because it is measured on what is left. The rise needed is the dollars lost divided by the dollars left. After a fall of 50%, $100.00 has become $50.00. Getting back takes $50.00 on $50.00, a rise of 100%.
Here is the rise that undoes each fall, from a start of $100.00. Rises are rounded to one decimal place. The bigger the fall, the more the rise has to be.

levels.title: The business cycle, bull and bear
learn: Name the four phases of the business cycle.
Tell a correction from a bear market by the fall from the peak.

cards.text: The economy moves in a cycle: it grows, stops, shrinks and starts again. Economists name four phases, in order. After a trough comes another expansion.

figure.title: The four phases
rows: The top, where growth stops and turns
The bottom, where it turns up

cards.text: A phase is told by which way things are moving, not by how high a number is. The same high number can belong to different phases, depending on whether it is still climbing or about to turn. The cycle repeats, but the length of each phase is not fixed.

Nobody rings a bell at the top or the bottom. A peak or a trough is only clear afterwards. Two words are used for markets. A bull market is one where prices are rising and people feel confident. A bear market is one where prices are falling and confidence has gone.
How far must prices fall to count as a bear market? The press uses a habit, not a law. Nobody enforces it. The fall is measured from the peak, not from the price you paid.

figure.title: Fall from the peak, and what the press calls it

cards.text: To find the fall from the peak, divide the drop by the peak: (peak - now) / peak. Say a made-up fund peaked at $50.00 and now sits at $42.00. The drop is $8.00, and $8.00 / $50.00 is 16%. That is a correction.

Bull and bear describe the market as a whole, not your own holdings. A market can fall less than 10% while one company in it falls 40%. Someone who bought near the bottom can be up while the market is still called a bear market. The label counts from the peak.

questions.label: Find the trough
questions.prompt: This line shows a made-up measure of how much the economy is producing, as a percent of its starting level. Tap the point that is the trough.
questions.hint: Look at the first card's table for what a trough is.
questions.why: Yes. The trough is the lowest point, before the line turns up. Here it is Month 7.
questions.miss: Check the first card's table for what a trough is.

questions.label: Which phase
questions.prompt: Jobs are being added, spending is rising and profits are growing. Which phase fits best?
questions.hint: Look at the table on the first card.

options.why: Yes. Growth, with more jobs and spending, is an expansion.
A contraction is when the economy shrinks, with fewer jobs and less spending.
A trough is the bottom, where it turns up. Here things are already growing.

questions.label: Level or direction
questions.prompt: Which tells you more about the phase: how high a number is, or which way it is moving?
questions.hint: The second card says what a phase is told by.

options.why: A high number can sit in different phases. The direction tells you more.
Yes. The same high number can sit in different phases, depending on its direction.
Direction matters. It helps tell the phases apart.

questions.label: Bull market
questions.prompt: Prices have been rising for months and people feel confident. Which word fits?
questions.hint: Third card: which market has rising prices?

options.why: A bear market is falling prices with confidence gone.
A correction is a fall, and here prices are rising.
Yes. Rising prices and confidence are a bull market.

questions.label: Fall from the peak
questions.prompt: A made-up fund peaked at $80.00 and now sits at $68.00. How many percent below its peak is it?
questions.hint: Divide the drop by the peak.
questions.why: Yes. The drop is $12.00, and $12.00 / $80.00 is 0.15, which is 15%.

traps.why: That is the drop in dollars. A percent needs a division by the peak.

questions.miss: The fall from the peak is the drop divided by the peak, not by the price now.

questions.label: What it is called
questions.prompt: A made-up fund is 24% below its peak. What does the press call a fall of that size?
questions.hint: Check the table of falls on the fourth card.

options.why: A correction is 10% or more but under 20%. This fall is bigger.
Yes. A fall of 20% or more from the peak is called a bear market.
A pullback is around 5%. This fall is much bigger.

questions.label: Where it starts
questions.prompt: A made-up fund peaked at $150.00. What price is exactly 20% below its peak, where a bear market begins?
questions.hint: Take 20% off the peak, not off any other price.
questions.why: Yes. 20% of $150.00 is $30.00, so the price is $120.00.

traps.why: That is the size of the drop. The question asks for the price.

questions.miss: Find 80% of the peak. That is what is left after a 20% fall.

questions.label: How firm
questions.prompt: How firm are the 10% and 20% lines for a correction and a bear market?
questions.hint: The fourth card says how they are used.

options.text: The market's habit, not a law
options.why: Yes. The press uses them, but nobody enforces them.
No one enforces them. They are a habit.

options.text: Set by each company for itself
options.why: No company sets them. They are the market's habit.

questions.label: Market and holdings
questions.prompt: The market has fallen only 6% from its peak. One company in it has fallen 40%. Which statement is true?
questions.hint: The last card says what bull and bear describe.

options.text: The market must be in a bear market, since one company fell 40%
options.why: One company does not decide the market. The fall of the whole market is what counts.

options.text: The market has not reached a correction, yet that company's owners lost a lot
options.why: Yes. The words describe the whole market. Owners of one company can lose far more.

options.text: The owners of that company lost nothing, since the market held up
options.why: The owners lost 40% of their holding. The market's fall does not change that.

questions.label: Back to the peak
questions.prompt: A made-up fund peaked at $200.00 and has fallen 25%. What percent rise from there gets it back to the peak? Round to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Dollars lost divided by dollars left, as in level 2.
questions.why: Yes. $200.00 falls to $150.00. Getting back takes $50.00 on $150.00, which is 33.3%.

traps.why: A rise of 25% on $150.00 adds only $37.50. The rise is measured on what is left.

questions.miss: Divide the dollars lost by the dollars left, as in the last level.

levels.title: Who pays the adviser
learn: Say who pays six kinds of investment adviser.
Ask what happens to an adviser's income if you lose money.

cards.text: If nobody can tell what phase the economy is in, plenty of people will tell you what to do. Before you weigh any advice, ask who pays the person giving it. That can be answered. "Do I trust them?" is only a feeling.
Here are six sources of advice and who pays each one. They are described by how they are paid. No real person or firm is meant.

figure.title: Six sources, and who pays them
rows: The bank, by salary and sales targets
You, a flat or hourly fee
You, small fees on each trade

cards.text: A bank adviser is paid by the bank, so what the adviser offers may be the bank's own products. A fee-only planner is paid by the client, a flat fee or by the hour, and no product pays the planner. Neither is simply good or bad. Each one's pay points somewhere.

A discount brokerage app gives you tools to trade, not advice. An influencer earns from advertisers, from affiliate links (links that pay the sender when you sign up or buy) and from the platform. A company's news release is written by the company, to make it look good.

A friend with a tip is paid by no one, which also means no one is accountable if it goes wrong. That does not make the tip better or worse. The same test works on every source: what happens to this person's income if I lose money?

That test replaces "is this person honest?", which you cannot see. It also keeps things fair: bank advisers have sales targets too, so this is not "banks good, influencers bad". On a website, a number you can check against its source is worth more than a conclusion you are asked to accept.

questions.prompt: Who pays a fee-only planner?
questions.hint: The table has a row for this source.

options.why: A fee-only planner is not paid by a bank. The client pays.

questions.hint: Who writes it, and why?

options.why: Yes. The company writes it, so it shows the good side.

options.why: It is written to make the company look good, not to help you choose.

questions.prompt: What does a discount brokerage app give you?
questions.hint: Fourth card.

options.why: A plan is advice. The app gives tools, not advice.
Yes. You pay small fees on trades, and the app gives tools, not advice.
A fee-only planner is a different source. The app gives tools to trade, not advice.

questions.label: The test question
questions.prompt: Which question works on any source of advice?
questions.hint: The fifth card gives it.

options.why: You cannot see honesty. Pay is something you can ask about.
Followers show reach, not whose income depends on what you do.

options.text: What happens to their income if I lose money?
options.why: Yes. It can be answered, and it shows where their pay points.

questions.label: Banks and pay
questions.prompt: Which statement is true, going by this level?
questions.hint: The last card says what the test is not.

options.text: A bank adviser has sales targets too, so the test applies there as well
options.why: Yes. Every source has pay that points somewhere, the bank's as well.

options.text: Bank advisers give advice that is free of pay pressures
options.why: A bank adviser has sales targets, so pay points somewhere.

options.text: Any source paid by the client is always right
options.why: Being paid by the client points the pay toward the client. It does not make the advice always right.

questions.label: Number or claim
questions.prompt: Which is the better thing to rely on from a website?
questions.hint: The last card ends on this.

options.text: A confident conclusion with no source
options.why: A conclusion with no source asks you to accept it.

options.text: A number you can check against its source
options.why: Yes. You can verify a number. A conclusion asks you to accept it.

options.text: A page that many people read
options.why: Many readers do not make a claim true.

levels.title: Reading a chart
learn: Read a trend, support and resistance on a price chart.
Say why a pattern on a chart is not proof of what comes next.

cards.text: A price chart is a line of past prices, oldest on the left. Traders have three words for what they see. A trend is the way the line is mostly heading: up, down or sideways.

Support is a price the line keeps bouncing up from, as if there were a floor. Resistance is a price the line keeps failing to climb past, as if there were a ceiling. Both are drawn afterwards, by looking at where the line turned before.

A made-up price starts at $40.00. Each day a coin is flipped: heads, up 5%; tails, down 5%. Each day's 5% is of that day's starting price. Prices are rounded to the cent. Seven flips drew this line. It looks like an uptrend, yet nothing but a coin made it.

figure.title: A price set by seven coin flips

cards.text: A coin has no memory, so after any run of heads the next flip is still even. Random moves can still draw lines that look like trends or clean bounces. A seller who is paid when you act has a reason to show only the best-looking few.

Charts are not useless. Real prices are not coin flips, and traders use charts to describe what has happened and to plan when they would get out. What the coin-flip line shows is narrower: seeing a pattern is not the same as knowing what comes next.

The Exchange puts a 12-month line on each card of its funds and town companies, with no numbers on the line itself. You can name its trend there. Read the price and the percent change on the card as well. The line describes the past. It does not say what the next month will do.

questions.label: A trend
questions.prompt: What is a trend on a price chart?
questions.hint: The first card defines it.

options.text: The way the line is mostly heading
options.why: Yes. A trend is the main direction: up, down or sideways.

options.text: A price the line keeps bouncing up from
options.why: That is support, not a trend.

options.text: A price the line cannot climb past
options.why: That is resistance, not a trend.

questions.label: A floor price
questions.prompt: A made-up price keeps dipping to $20.00 and bouncing back up. What is $20.00 called?
questions.hint: The line is bouncing up from this price.

options.why: Resistance is a ceiling the line fails to climb past. Here the line bounces up from the price.
Yes. A price the line keeps bouncing up from is support.
A trend is the line's main direction, not a single price.

questions.label: A ceiling price
questions.prompt: A made-up price keeps climbing to $55.00 and turning back down. What is $55.00 called?
questions.hint: The line turns back down from this price.

options.why: Support is a floor. Here the price turns back down from $55.00, so it is a ceiling.
A pullback is a fall of around 5% from the peak. It is not a name for a price the line turns from.
Yes. A price the line keeps failing to climb past is resistance.

questions.label: The next flip
questions.prompt: A coin-flip price has gone up five days in a row. What is the chance that the next flip is heads?
questions.hint: The fourth card says what a coin has.

options.text: Higher, since it is on a run
options.why: A run does not change the coin. The next flip is still even.

options.text: Still even: the coin has no memory
options.why: Yes. Each flip is 50-50, whatever came before.
The coin does not owe tails. The next flip is still even.

questions.label: Best-looking few
questions.prompt: A seller shows you a chart that looks like a perfect trend, picked from many random ones. What does it show?
questions.hint: Think about how the chart was chosen.

options.text: How some random charts happen to look
options.why: Yes. Random moves can look like a clean trend by luck.

options.text: That a pattern predicts the next move
options.why: They were chosen for how they look. That does not show a pattern predicts.

options.text: That coin flips follow a plan
options.why: A coin has no plan. A chosen chart shows luck.

questions.label: Up, then down
questions.prompt: A made-up price is $100.00. One day it rises 10%. The next day it falls 10%. What is it worth after both days, in dollars?
questions.hint: The second move is a percent of the price after the first.
questions.why: Yes. $110.00 after the rise, then 10% of that is $11.00, so $99.00.

traps.why: The two moves do not cancel. The fall is measured on the higher price.

questions.miss: Do the rise first. Then take 10% off the new price.

questions.label: Two tails
questions.prompt: A made-up price is $50.00. A coin sends it down 20% on two days in a row. What is it worth after both days, in dollars?
questions.hint: The second 20% is of the price after the first fall.
questions.why: Yes. $40.00 after the first day, then 20% of that is $8.00, leaving $32.00.

traps.why: That takes 40% off the start. The second 20% is of the lower price.

questions.miss: Take the first 20% off. Then take 20% off what is left.

questions.label: First fall
questions.prompt: This made-up price was set by coin flips from a start of $50.00, up or down 4% a day. Tap the first point that is lower than the point before it.

figure.title: A price set by seven coin flips

questions.hint: Read the line from the left.
questions.why: Yes. The price rose for three days and first fell on Day 4.
questions.miss: Compare each day with the day before it.

questions.label: Charts, not useless
questions.prompt: Which statement is true, going by this level?
questions.hint: The fifth card says what the coin-flip line shows.

options.text: Seeing a pattern is not the same as knowing what comes next
options.why: Yes. Patterns show up even in coin flips.

options.text: Charts are useless and should be ignored
options.why: Charts can describe what happened. They do not say what comes next.
Real prices are not coin flips. The coin-flip chart only shows that patterns can appear in noise.

questions.label: Who shows it
questions.prompt: Which person has a money reason to show you only the best-looking chart?
questions.hint: The fourth card says who has the reason.

options.text: Someone who draws charts as a hobby and sells nothing
options.why: Someone who sells nothing has no money reason. The card points to a seller paid when you act.

options.text: A seller who is paid when you act
options.why: Yes. A seller paid when you act has a reason to show only the best-looking few.

options.text: A reader looking at a free chart
options.why: A reader is not paid when you act. The card points to a seller.

units.title: Lending your money
units.blurb: Savings accounts, GICs, T-bills and bonds, and why bond prices move.

levels.title: Four ways to lend
learn: Name the four common ways to lend money.
Say who you lend to, for how long, and how you are paid.

cards.text: Lending means letting someone else use your money for a while. They promise to pay it back, and they pay you for the loan. Four common ways to lend are a savings account, a GIC, a T-bill and a bond. Each one answers three questions: who, for how long, and how you get paid.
The table puts the four side by side. Read across a row to see who you lend to, for how long, and how you are paid. The next cards take them one at a time.

figure.title: Four ways to lend
rows: You pay less, get face value
A coupon each year, then face value

cards.text: A savings account and a GIC are both loans to a bank. You can take money out of a savings account at any time with no penalty. A GIC runs for a set term and is locked in. In this example, $2,500.00 in a GIC at 3% earns $75.00 in one year.

A T-bill is a short loan to a government, such as for 3 months. It pays no interest. You buy it for less than its face value, here $1,000.00, and you get the full face value back at the end. Your gain is the gap. Buy at $985.00 and you gain $15.00.

A bond is a loan to a government or a company for a number of years. It pays a coupon, a fixed payment, once a year in these examples. At the end, the maturity, you get the face value back. A $1,000.00 bond with a 4% coupon pays $40.00 a year for its years, then returns the $1,000.00.

A bond can be sold to another buyer before it ends. A debenture is a company bond backed only by the company’s promise to pay, with no asset behind it. Level 2 asks how safe each way is. Level 3 asks what a bond sells for.

questions.label: Cash out any time
questions.prompt: Which of the four can you cash out tomorrow with no penalty?

terms.meaning: A loan to a bank for a set term, at a set rate. Usually locked in.

questions.hint: Look at the “For how long” column of the table on the second card.

options.why: A GIC runs for a set term and is locked in until the term ends.
Yes. Money in a savings account can come out at any time with no penalty.
A T-bill pays its face value at its end date. It is short, but it is not an any-time account.
A bond runs for years and pays back its face value at the end.

questions.label: How a T-bill pays
questions.prompt: How does a T-bill pay you?

terms.meaning: A short loan to a government. It pays no interest: you buy it for less than its face value.
The amount a bond or T-bill pays back at the end.

options.why: That is how a bond pays. A T-bill pays no coupon.

options.why: That is how a savings account works. A T-bill has no balance that grows.

options.text: You pay less than face value and get the full face value back
options.why: Yes. The gap between what you pay and the face value is your gain.

options.text: Interest at a set rate on a locked term
options.why: That is a GIC. A T-bill pays no interest at all.

questions.prompt: Sana puts $4,000.00 in a GIC at 3% for one year. How much interest does she earn?

terms.meaning: A short loan to a government. It pays no interest: you buy it for less than its face value.

options.why: Yes. No asset sits behind it, only the company’s promise.

options.why: That describes a T-bill, which pays its gain as the gap between price and face value.

options.why: A savings account is a loan to a bank, not a bond from a company.

questions.prompt: Use the table. Which way to lend can be a loan to a company that is not a bank?

figure.title: Four ways to lend
rows: You pay less, get face value
A coupon each year, then face value

questions.hint: Read the “You lend to” column.

options.why: The table shows a T-bill as a loan to a government.
The table shows a savings account as a loan to a bank.
The table shows a GIC as a loan to a bank.
Yes. The table says a bond is a loan to a government or a company.

levels.title: Safe, locked or both
learn: Say why a riskier borrower pays a higher rate.
Say what deposit insurance and a GIC do and do not cover.

cards.text: Lenders ask for more when a borrower is more likely not to pay back. A government is among the safest to lend to. A new business with no sales history is among the riskiest. The rate is the price of the risk: the riskier the borrower, the higher the rate asked.

If a bank fails, deposit insurance helps you get your deposit back, up to a limit. In Canada, CDIC is the deposit insurer for banks. The limit and what is covered can change, so check the insurer’s own website. A credit union has its own insurer, so check that one. A bond is not a deposit.

A GIC is guaranteed, but guaranteed does not mean no risk. The guarantee is your principal and the stated rate, in dollars, for the set term. It does not promise that the rate beats rising prices. It does not promise you will not miss a better rate. It does not let you out early.

Mina puts $1,000.00 in a 5-year GIC at 4%. It pays $40.00 a year. A year later, new GICs pay 6%, which would be $60.00 a year. Her GIC has no price that can fall, but she cannot leave. She is locked in at 4% while the market pays 6%, which is $20.00 a year less.

Cash is money you can spend now. A cash equivalent is a very safe, short-term place that turns into cash fast, such as a savings account or a short T-bill. A five-year GIC is grouped with cash but is slow to get out of: not a true cash equivalent. Safety and how fast you can get out are two different questions.

In the Net Worth building you can hold a savings account and buy a GIC for 12, 36 or 60 months, from $100.00. Savings money is there at any time. A GIC is locked: you cannot take it out early. The game starts the savings rate at 2.75% a year. It can change, so read the live rate there.

questions.label: Highest rate asked
questions.prompt: Which borrower would have to offer the highest rate to get a loan?
questions.hint: The rate is the price of the risk. Which borrower is riskiest?

options.text: A government with a long record of paying
options.why: A government is among the safest to lend to, so it can borrow at a lower rate.

options.text: A bank that has paid lenders for years
options.why: A long record of paying back makes a lender ask for less.

options.text: A new business with no sales history
options.why: Yes. A lender cannot be sure a new business will pay back, so it asks for more.

options.text: A province with a long record
options.why: Like a federal government, a province with a long record is a safer borrower.

cards.text: A bond does not have to be held to the end. Its owner can sell it to another buyer. What a buyer will pay depends on what new bonds pay today, the market yield. Ayo owns a 5-year bond with a $1,000.00 face value and a 4% coupon: $40.00 a year.

Rates rise to 6%. A new $1,000.00 bond now pays $60.00 a year. No one pays $1,000.00 for Ayo’s $40.00 a year when $60.00 is on offer. So the price of his bond falls below face value, a discount. If rates fall, the price rises above face value, a premium.

A price is what the payments are worth today. A payment is worth less today than when it arrives, because you could earn the market yield while you wait. Divide it by 1.06 for each year, at 6%. Coupons here come once a year. A 1-year bond pays $1,040.00: $1,040.00 / 1.06 = $981.13.

For the 5-year bond, divide each coupon by 1.06 for as many years as it waits, and do the same for the $1,000.00 at the end. Add up what they are worth today. The class example gives $915.75. That is $84.25 below face value.

levels.title: Three ways to own
learn: Tell a stock, a mutual fund and an ETF apart.
Say what a fund holds and who chooses it.

cards.text: You can own a piece of the market in three ways. You can buy one company's stock. You can buy a mutual fund. Or you can buy an ETF. A stock is a share of one company. This level shows how the three differ.
A fund is a basket. One purchase holds many companies at once. Omar puts $1,200 into a fund that holds 60 companies in equal parts. In this simple picture, $20.00 of his money goes to each company.

A mutual fund and an ETF both hold a basket. The difference is how they trade. A mutual fund has one price a day. An ETF trades like a stock: its price changes all day while the market is open. A stock also changes all day.

Someone decides what goes in a fund: a manager who picks, or a rule. An index is a list, such as the 60 biggest companies in a country. An index fund follows the list and makes no picks, so it usually costs less.
Here are the three side by side. A fund charges a yearly fee, and the next levels show what it does to your money. A stock has no fund fee.
In the game's Exchange, prices move once a world month. Its funds have a ticker and a buy price and a sell price, like a stock, so they work like ETFs. Look at them on the Exchange.

cards.text: Funds differ in what is in the basket. Five common kinds are money market, bond, index, actively managed and balanced. To tell them apart, ask one question: what does the fund hold?
Here are the five kinds and what each holds. A bond is a loan to a government or a company. A treasury bill is a short loan to a government. A stock fund can follow a list or have a manager pick.

cards.text: A money market fund holds treasury bills and other short-term loans, and it aims to keep your money steady. It counts as a cash equivalent. A bond fund holds government and company bonds. Both hold loans, not shares of companies.

An index fund holds the companies on a list in the same weights as the list, and picks nothing. An actively managed fund has a manager who chooses, say, 30 stocks the manager expects to beat the market. Such funds usually charge more.

A balanced fund holds stocks and bonds in a set mix, such as 60% stocks and 40% bonds. When stocks rise, the stock part grows past 60%. Rebalancing moves money back to the set mix. A balanced fund does this for you.
The Exchange has three funds. DAAX holds every company in town. DAAB holds bonds. DAAG is 60% DAAX and 40% DAAB, rebalanced every month, so it is a balanced fund. It has no money market fund.

cards.text: A fund charges a yearly fee called the MER, the management expense ratio. It is a percent of what you hold in the fund. It is taken out of the fund's return before you see the return, so no bill ever arrives.
Say you hold $10,000 in Fund C, which charges 2.25% a year. The fee for the year is 2.25% of $10,000, which is $225.00. You do not write a cheque. Your fund simply earns less.

So you can count the fee as coming off the return. Say the market earns 6% in a year and Fund C charges 2.25%. You keep 6% - 2.25% = 3.75%. Real funds take the fee a little at a time, so this is a close, simple way to count it.
Funds A, B and C are made-up funds for this unit. Here is what each one lets you keep when the market earns 6% in a year. The bigger the fee, the less you keep.

A fund's own page lists its MER. Use the fund company's page, not a news article, since articles quote old numbers. A past return only shows how one period went, and it does not promise the next. You cannot know a future return, but you can read what a fund charges.
The Exchange puts a Fund fee (MER) line on each fund's card. The game starts with 0.06% a year for DAAX, 0.10% for DAAB and 0.20% for DAAG. The fee comes off the price a little each month.

levels.title: What a fee takes over time
learn: Work out how a fee grows into a big gap, year by year.

cards.text: The class example: $10,000 is invested once and left for 30 years. The market earns 6% a year. Fund C charges 2.25%, so it keeps 3.75%, and each year the balance is multiplied by 1.0375. Year 1: $10,375.00. Year 2: $10,764.06.
Each year, the money grows on last year's balance. Here are both balances every five years, rounded to the dollar. Both grow, but Fund C grows slower, and the gap widens.
Funds A and B charge 0.25% and 1.00%. At year 30, no fee gives $57,435, Fund A $53,507, Fund B $43,219 and Fund C $30,175. Fund C ends $27,260 below no fee, which is 47.5% less.

The longer you hold, the more a fee takes. After 10 years, Fund C has $14,450 against $17,908 with no fee: 19.3% less. After 30 years it is 47.5% less. The fee is paid every year, and the money it takes stops growing too.

The fee does not shrink when returns do. If the market earns only 3%, Fund C still charges 2.25% and you keep 0.75%. The fee takes 75% of that year's return, not 37.5%. Over 30 years $10,000 ends at $12,513, against $24,273 with no fee.

A fee also slows doubling. The Rule of 72 estimates it: divide 72 by the yearly percent to get the years. At 6% that is 72 / 6 = 12 years. A 2% fee leaves 4%, and 72 / 4 = 18 years. The fee takes a third of the return but adds six years of waiting.

units.title: Diversification and the mix
units.blurb: Two kinds of risk, spreading out, and what a crash does to a mix.

levels.title: Two kinds of risk
learn: Say what happens to a mix when one company fails and when a whole market falls.

cards.text: Maya has $10,000 and puts the same amount into each company she owns. Suppose one company goes bankrupt and what she put in it is lost. Each company gets $10,000 divided by the number of companies. The numbers are made up for this example.

That is company risk: the chance that one company does badly or fails, whatever the rest of the market does. A bankruptcy, a recall or a fire can cause it. Owning more companies shrinks it, because each one becomes a smaller slice of your money.

A different event. The whole Canadian market falls 20% and every other market stays flat. Dev owns 50 Canadian companies, $200 in each, $10,000 in all. All 50 fall together, so he loses 20% of $10,000, which is $2,000. Owning 50 companies did not help him.

That is market risk: the chance that a whole market falls and takes its companies down together. What lowers it is spreading across places that do not fall together. The same $10,000 is below with less of it in Canada. The loss is the share in Canada times 20%.

Spreading out has limits. If every market falls at once, no place stays flat and a mix still loses. It also does not raise what you can expect to earn. It narrows the range of results you might land in: fewer very bad years and fewer very good ones.

So there are two jobs. More companies shrink company risk. More places, and more kinds of companies, shrink market risk. A mix of 200 companies that are all in one country has done the first job and very little of the second.

levels.title: Four ways to spread

cards.text: A mix can be spread out in four ways: by size, by style, by sector and by geography. A mix can be spread in one way and bunched in another. This level goes through the four, then reads a small mix.

Size is how big a company is: large or small. Style is how the market prices it. A growth company sells at a high price because buyers expect fast growth. A value company sells at a low price compared with what it earns. Nobody knows in advance which does better, so a mix may hold both.

A sector is a group of companies that do similar business. Four groups: interest sensitive (banks and others whose business moves with interest rates), consumer (sells to everyday shoppers), industrial (builds and moves things) and resources (oil, mines, forests).

Geography is where a company is based and does business: Canada, the United States, other countries (international) and emerging markets, which are countries whose markets are younger and growing fast. Companies in one country tend to rise and fall together.
Here is a made-up mix of five companies with $2,000 in each. Read it one way at a time: by sector, by size and by country.

Read by country: four of the five are in Canada, so the mix is bunched there. Read by size: four large and one small. Companies in the same sector also tend to fall together, so two bank shares count as two companies but move almost like one.

cards.text: A fund is one purchase that holds many companies at once. Each company it holds is a holding. Three facts on its page say most: how many holdings it has, its largest sector and that sector's weight, and what share of its money sits in each country. A weight is a share of the money, as a percent.
Here are three made-up funds. Read the three facts off each row. No real fund is described.

Fund R has 200 holdings, so one company failing barely shows. But 97% of its money is in Canada. If Canada falls 20% and other markets stay flat, Fund R falls about 97% x 20%, which is 19.4%. Many holdings fix company risk. They do not fix market risk.

Is a fund of 200 Canadian companies diversified? Partly: it is spread across companies, not across countries. Funds can also be bunched in the same way. Two funds that are both mostly banks look like two holdings but move almost like one, because banks tend to fall together.

You can mix funds. The share of a mix in Canada is each fund's Canada share times its weight in your money, added up. Put 50% in Fund R and 50% in Fund S: 50% x 97% + 50% x 3% = 48.5% + 1.5% = 50%. Half of the money is in Canada.

Real funds show these numbers on their own pages, usually with a date. Write down the page and the date next to each number you copy, because what a fund holds can change. The numbers on these cards are made up.

cards.text: A mix has parts that earn different returns. Its blended return is worked out from each part and how much money is in it. It is not the middle of the returns. Picture a see-saw: the balance point sits closer to the end that holds more money.

Here is the class example, with made-up rates. The $10,000 earns $640 + $60 = $700 in a year, which is 7%. The stocks part holds most of the money, so the whole earns 7%, close to the stocks rate of 8%. The middle of 8% and 3% would be 5.5%, which is wrong.

figure.title: Stocks and cash, rates made up

cards.text: A shortcut gives the same answer, and it is the step you used to blend funds: weight times value, added up. Multiply each part's weight by its return and add. For 80% stocks at 8% and 20% cash at 3%: 80% x 8% + 20% x 3% = 6.4% + 0.6% = 7.0%. The weights add up to 100%. A mix never earns more than its best part.

Real estate can be a part of a mix. A REIT, a real estate investment trust, owns buildings that earn rent, such as apartments, warehouses and offices. You buy units like shares. It pays most of its rent out to its owners as distributions, often every month.

A REIT's return is its yield plus the change in the price of its units. The yield is the yearly payout as a percent of the price. The price can fall, so the payout is not the whole return. Here is a three-part mix with made-up rates.

figure.title: A three-part mix, rates made up

cards.text: For that mix: 50% x 8% + 30% x 4% + 20% x 6% = 4.0% + 1.2% + 1.2% = 6.4%. Check that the weights add up to 100% before you start. Moving money toward the part with the higher return raises the blend. The next level shows what that can cost.

levels.title: The Rule of 72 and where it is rough
learn: Use the Rule of 72 forwards and backwards.
Say where the rule is close to the exact time and where it is rough.

cards.text: The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double: years = 72 divided by the yearly rate. At 6% that is 72 / 6 = 12 years. It also runs backwards. Money that doubled in 6 years grew at about 72 / 6 = 12% a year. The rule is for one lump of money with nothing added or taken out.

One guess is 100 / 6, about 17 years, as if every year added 6% of the first $10,000. But year two’s interest is on a bigger balance, so the wait is shorter. Here is $10,000 at 6%, multiplied by 1.06 each year, to the nearest dollar. It passes $20,000 in year 12.
The exact doubling time at 6% is a little under 12 years: about 11.9. A calculator or spreadsheet finds it. The rule says 12, a very close estimate. Here are both at six example rates, in years.

Read the gap. At 6%, 9% and 12% the rule is within about 0.1 of a year. At 1% it says 72 years, but the exact time is 69.7, about 2 years too long. At 24% it says 3 years and the exact time is 3.2, a little too short. At very low or very high rates, treat the rule as rougher.

Interest is not always added once a year. Say 6% a year is added monthly: 0.5% each month, 144 months in 12 years. $10,000 grows to 10,000 x 1.005^144 = $20,508, a bit more than $20,000. Doubling takes about 11.6 years, not 12. The rule is still a good first check.

levels.title: Growing with regular deposits
learn: Follow a balance month by month when deposits go in.
Use the shortcut and see what a bigger deposit, rate or time does.

cards.text: Most people add money every month. Each month the balance grows by that month’s interest, then the deposit goes in at the end of the month. At 6% a year the monthly rate is 6% divided by 12, which is 0.5%, so the balance is multiplied by 1.005. Here are the first three months of $100 deposits.

Do this 120 times and you have ten years of $100 deposits. You put in $12,000 and the balance is $16,388. The rest, $4,388, is interest. The longer it runs, the bigger the interest share. A spreadsheet’s future value function adds up the chain for you.

A shortcut saves 120 steps. Balance = deposit x (1.005^n - 1) / 0.005, where n is the number of months and 0.005 is the monthly rate. Two slips to avoid: typing 6% where 0.5% a month belongs, and typing 10 for n when ten years is 120 months. Rates here are examples.

A lump sum and monthly deposits can be added together. Start with $10,000 and add $100 a month for 12 years at 6%. The lump grows alone, the deposits grow alone, and the two add up. The Rule of 72 describes only the lump: it knows nothing about the money you add later.

What helps most: a bigger deposit, a higher rate or more years? Here are three plans for 20 years of saving. A higher deposit and a higher rate both help. So does time, because it lets interest earn interest for longer. These rates are examples, not forecasts.

levels.title: Inflation grows your costs
learn: Grow a bill to a later year at an example inflation rate.

cards.text: Inflation is a rise in prices over time, so the same bills cost more. Costs grow the way money does: each year you multiply by 1 plus the rate. Take Mia’s bills, $3,000 a month today. If prices rise 2% a year (an example rate), next year they are $3,000 x 1.02 = $3,060.00.

Over 33 years you multiply by 1.02 thirty-three times. That is 1.02^33, about 1.92. Mia’s $3,000 of bills becomes $5,766.69 a month. A common slip is to add 2% thirty-three times, which is 66%, and get $4,980.00. That misses that each rise is on prices that already rose.

One point of inflation changes the answer a lot. Here is the same $3,000 a month after 33 years at three example rates. A small difference in rate, repeated for many years, becomes a large difference in dollars.

The Rule of 72 works on prices too: divide 72 by the inflation rate. At 2%, prices double in about 72 / 2 = 36 years. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation near 2%, the midpoint of a range from 1% to 3%. That is its target.

Costs and income must be compared in the same year’s dollars. Mia expects $4,500 a month in 33 years. That is more than $3,000, so it looks safe. But her bills will be $5,766.69 by then, which is $1,266.69 more than her income.

cards.text: A statement counts dollars. That is the nominal amount. Real means what the money buys after prices rise. Take $200,000 in a GIC at 3% for 10 years, with prices rising 3% a year (a class example). The statement grows to $268,783. Prices grew just as much, so it still buys only $200,000 of today’s goods.

Real return = (1 + rate) / (1 + inflation) - 1. At a 3% rate and 3% inflation that is 1.03 / 1.03 - 1 = 0, so you run in place. Dollars on the statement divided by (1 + inflation) for each year gives what they buy today. Here is the same GIC at three inflation rates.

A shortcut is rate minus inflation: 3% - 5% = -2%, near the exact -1.9%. It drifts at bigger rates: at 8% and 5% it says 3.0%, but the exact answer is 2.9%. The game shows both numbers: the Bank of DAA lists a savings rate and the inflation rate. The game starts at 2.75% and 2.1%, and the teacher can change them.

The Rule of 72 can run on the real return. A 6% fund with 2% inflation has a real return of about 4%, so what it buys doubles in about 72 / 4 = 18 years. The dollars double sooner, in about 12 years, but each dollar buys less by then. Doubled dollars are not doubled buying power.

levels.title: Percent change and short stretches
learn: Find a percent change and a new price from one.
Say why a short stretch is only a sample.

cards.text: Percent change says how far a price moved as a share of where it started: (latest - start) / start x 100. A price goes from $50.00 to $56.00. The change is $6.00, and $6.00 / $50.00 = 0.12, which is 12%. A fall is the same sum with a minus sign. Divide by the start, not the latest.

You can run it the other way. A $60.00 price that rises 10% gains $6.00 and becomes $66.00. One that falls 10% loses $6.00 and becomes $54.00. A rise of 10% and then a fall of 10% does not get you back: $66.00 x 0.90 = $59.40, because the fall is 10% of a bigger price.

A percent change covers whatever stretch you measure. A price that goes from $1,000.00 to $1,300.00 over 4 years has changed 30% in total. That is not 30% a year. Always say how long the stretch was before you compare two changes.

A short stretch is a sample, not a verdict. Here is a made-up price that starts at $50.00. After week 2 it is up 8% from the start. After week 4 it is down 5% from the start. After week 6 it is up 4% from the start. Stop on a different week and you tell a different story.

units.title: Investing with values
units.blurb: Three ways to invest by your values, and who a choice affects.

levels.title: Three ways to invest by values
learn: Tell the three ways to invest by your values apart.
Say what a screen is, and what each way keeps or leaves out.

cards.text: Ethical investing means choosing investments by your values as well as by what they might earn. An investor does this with a screen: a rule plus facts about each company. The rule says what to look for. The facts tell you which companies pass.

The first way is to exclude. You leave out companies that do something you will not own. The rule could be “no animal testing”. A fund that says “we own no weapons makers” is excluding. Every company that passes the rule stays in.

The second way is best in class. You keep every kind of business, but in each kind you own only the companies with the best scores. The rule is about ranking. It compares a company only with others of its own kind.

The third way is to own and vote. You keep the company and use what an owner has: a vote at its annual meeting. You are trying to change the company from inside, not to leave it. A shareholder is an owner of shares.
Side by side, the three ways all start from the investor’s values. They differ in what the investor does about a company.

levels.title: Whose values, and who a choice touches
learn: Say whose values set a screen, and why two investors can choose different ones.
Name who a share touches, and who gets the money when you buy one.

cards.text: Whose values set the screen? The investor’s. If an adviser helps, the values are the client’s. There is no one official list of ethical companies that every investor follows. Two people can read the same facts and still pick different rules, because they care about different things.

Rina and Joel each have $12,000 and the same eight companies. Rina’s rule is “no animal testing”. Joel’s rule is “no more than 15% of waste sent to landfill”. Each splits the money equally over the companies that pass. Same facts, different rules, different lists.
These are the facts both rules use. Rina’s rule leaves out every company marked Yes. Joel’s leaves out every company above 15%. Reading the table is counting, and counting can be checked.

Facts and values are different questions. “How many companies does this rule leave out?” is a fact: you count them. “Which rule should an investor use?” depends on what the investor values. A table can answer the first. It cannot settle the second.

A share touches people. An owner shares in how the company earns, can vote at its annual meeting, and helps set its price. If many investors will not buy a share, its price can fall, and selling new shares to raise money can get harder.

Who gets your money when you buy a share? Not the company. An exchange matches you with an investor who is selling, and that investor is paid. The company got its money once, when it first sold the share. It is like buying a used bike from its owner: the shop gets nothing.

learn: Show how a narrower screen changes the money in each company and the kinds of business left.

cards.text: Rina’s eight companies again, now with the facts a landfill limit and a best-in-class rule use. Glimmer Lane Cosmetics and Northcote Pharmacy Labs are the two that test on animals. Scores are out of 100 and made up.

A screen has a cost: fewer companies. A 25% landfill limit leaves out Alder Stitch Apparel (40%) and Cedarline Paper (28%). Six are left. Rina’s $12,000 now goes equally into six: $12,000 / 6 = $2,000 in each, up from $1,500.
A screen can also take out a whole kind of business. Under a 15% landfill limit, both clothing companies are over the limit (40% and 20%). Rina would own no clothing company at all.

Best in class keeps the top score in each kind: Fernhill Soap Works, Willow Clinic Supplies, Birchmoor Outfitters and Riverbend Printing. The top scorer in a kind is only the best of its own group, not a company with nothing a rule would worry about.

A screen only sees the facts it is given. “No animal testing” keeps Fernhill Soap Works, which does no testing itself but buys its main ingredient from a lab that does. A 15% limit keeps Riverbend Printing, whose share of waste is small but whose total is large. The data did not measure those things.

A fund that applies a values screen is often called an ethical fund. A fund’s name states its aim. Its list of exclusions and its holdings show what it does. In the Exchange, every fund and stock has a short note. None of those notes mentions a values screen.

options.text: The total amount of waste it sends to landfill
options.why: A small share can still be a large amount if the company makes a lot of waste.

options.text: That it tests products on animals
options.why: The table shows it does not test, and the limit does not use testing.
Its score is high, and the limit does not use scores.

options.text: That it is in the Paper kind
options.why: The kind is in the table. The limit just does not use it.

questions.label: Label or holdings
questions.prompt: A fund’s name says it is “responsible”. What shows what its screen actually does?
questions.hint: Read the last card.

options.why: A name is only a label. It does not list what the fund leaves out.
A price tells you nothing about what the screen leaves out.
A fee is a cost. It does not show what the fund holds or leaves out.

options.text: Its list of exclusions and what it holds
options.why: A name states an aim. The exclusions and holdings show what the screen does.

questions.label: One bet weighs more
questions.prompt: A screen takes Rina from eight companies to four. What follows for her money?

terms.meaning: Spreading your money over many companies and over different kinds of business, so one going bad hurts less.

questions.hint: Think about how diversification works: one company is one bet.

options.text: Her money is spread more widely than before
options.why: Four companies spread the money less widely than eight.

options.text: Risk is gone because the companies were chosen with care
options.why: A screen chooses by values and facts. Fewer companies still means each one weighs more.

options.text: Each company holds more, so one company’s bad news matters more
options.why: The same money sits in fewer companies, so it is spread less widely.

options.text: Each company now holds less money
options.why: The same total is shared by fewer companies, so each holds more.
